reconstructed_article: The Victorian Government approved a $380 million wind farm at Mount Gellibrand in the state’s south-west. Planning Minister Rob Hulls announced the decision, stating the project is Australia’s most powerful and Victoria’s largest wind farm to date. The project is expected to create between 110 and 120 jobs during construction and up to 25 full-time positions during operation. The wind farm will be located 120 km west of Melbourne, near Colac. It will comprise 116 turbines of the 2 MW class, with an overall capacity of 232 MW. The facility is expected to produce over 700,000 MWh annually, enough to supply approximately 132,000 Victorian households. German company Pro Ventum International is undertaking the project. Minister Hulls said nine objections had been lodged against the project. Local landowner Tim Gore, who plans to have 32 turbines on his property, said he was not concerned about potential noise. Pro Ventum International said it would commence work on an Environmental Management report in the coming weeks. Wind farm critic Tim Le Roy said there was no environmental benefit from the project and the Victorian Government would better spend its money elsewhere. In October of the previous year, Colac Otway Council chief executive officer Tracey Slatter said the proposal would benefit the shire by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and addressing increasing energy demand.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo, Japan, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages from the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers. The class action is the first in Japan related to health damages caused by asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas. They claim that the government and manufacturers knew of the dangers of asbestos inhalation but failed to take proper precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died. Plaintiffs argue that the government and health ministry did not act quickly enough after international organizations issued warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen. They also blame the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for approving asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law. Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. Following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, the government implemented a 2006 law providing monetary assistance to victims and relatives. Plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted swimming near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. reported the sighting. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially identified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., the whales were guided back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. reported the sighting. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, deployed dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales washed up in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females—one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. said this was the worst stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., the whales were guided back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: American botanist Lou Jost discovered a new orchid species in a nature reserve in eastern Ecuador. The orchid has flowers measuring 2.1mm wide and transparent petals that are one cell thick. This species surpasses the previous record holder, Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species accidentally while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as Platystele jungermannioides. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, airborne asbestos was discovered in Renaissance Middle School in Montclair, New Jersey, prompting the evacuation of over 200 students and the school’s closure. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, was closed Monday and remained closed Tuesday while undergoing asbestos testing and cleaning. According to a letter sent to parents by the Superintendent’s Office of Montclair Public Schools, plaster may have been disturbed during construction on new fire doors on Thursday. An inspection arranged by the school district indicated asbestos was present in the plaster, and a subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates revealed airborne asbestos fiber levels exceeding the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan stated that testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting between parents and district officials, parents requested lockers be included in the cleanup, leading to the school’s closure on Tuesday. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at over six times acceptable levels. He stated the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building, was inadequate. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness stated the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

Tropical Storm Danielle has strengthened into a hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 130 km/h (80 mph). The storm is approaching Bermuda. Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami, Florida expect it to strengthen further over the next two days. Hurricane Danielle is the second hurricane of the 2010 Atlantic hurricane season. It formed near the Cape Verde Islands off the coast of West Africa and was initially classified as Tropical Depression Six before developing into a more organized cyclone. Meteorologists predict Danielle will be the first of several storms to form within the next two weeks, as the Atlantic hurricane season reaches its peak. Rick Knabb of the National Hurricane Center said, “There are signs that the Atlantic is acting like it should in August and September. We're seeing more activity than we did earlier in the season.”  

Tropical Storm Frank, an 80 km/h (50 mph) storm in the Pacific Ocean, is located about 210 km (130 miles) south-southwest of Acapulco, Mexico. Mexico has issued a tropical storm watch for the area.  

Although the 2010 Atlantic hurricane season appears to be one with low activity, emergency officials continue to stress safety and awareness to residents in hurricane-prone areas. Lauren McKeague of the Florida Division of Emergency Management said, “It only takes one storm to cause a loss of lives and devastating property damage.” Hurricane Andrew was cited as a catastrophic Category 5 storm that occurred during a lower-than-average season.

reconstructed_article: Thirteen Asian countries pledged on Friday to double the wild tiger population on the continent to 7,000 by 2022. The pledge was made in Thailand at Asia’s first ministerial conference on tiger conservation. The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam—countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found. Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva stated in a video address that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it. The meeting was partially organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups. Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand’s minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared to about 3,500 today. According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago, according to Voice of America. WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found. Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva stated in a video address that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it. The meeting was partially organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups. Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared to about 3,500 today. According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago, according to Voice of America. WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

Senator Campbell said the cutback means fewer bags in the litter stream and that the goal is to stop plastic bags entering the litter stream and spoiling Australia's environment. He said the result came from voluntary action by supermarkets and shoppers, with no regulations, levies, or additional costs to shoppers. Major supermarkets are committed to achieving a 50 per cent reduction goal by the end of this year. Campbell also said development of a viable degradable bag to replace existing lightweight plastic ones is key to further reductions. Environmentalists say plastic bags have had a severe impact on Australia's natural environment. Plastic bags can take between 20 and 1000 years to break down. An estimated 6.67 billion or 36,700 tonnes of plastic bags are disposed of in landfill sites throughout Australia each year. Many thousands of marine mammals and seabirds die every year worldwide as a result of plastic litter. A 2004 NSW Parliamentary paper reported that plastic bags are of significant concern in the marine and aquatic environment, as aquatic life can be threatened through entanglement, suffocation, and ingestion.

reconstructed_article: Joe Arpaio, Sheriff for Maricopa County, Arizona, is expected to endorse Republican presidential candidate Rick Perry of Texas at a New Hampshire campaign event, according to sources. Arpaio is expected to appear with Perry today and will remain in the state for three days. Arpaio refers to himself as “America’s Toughest Sheriff.” As Sheriff, he has led raids to arrest illegal immigrants and supported Arizona’s stringent immigration law. GOP presidential candidates Michele Bachmann, Herman Cain, and Mitt Romney actively sought his endorsement. He endorsed Romney in 2008. The endorsement could help Perry with voters who have had concerns about his record on illegal immigration. Perry was criticized for signing a bill granting in-state tuition benefits to college-age illegal immigrants. He defended the bill during a September presidential debate, saying those criticizing him “don’t have a heart.” He later backed down from the statement. As Governor of Texas for eleven years, Perry oversaw the state with the longest border with Mexico. He vetoed a bill that would have allowed illegal immigrants to receive driver’s licenses and signed another requiring identification to vote. During his presidential campaign, Perry opposed the proposed full-length border fence, calling it impractical. He favors targeted fencing combined with mobilization of enforcement personnel.

reconstructed_article:
The Australian Government is constructing a $210 million, 800-bed detention facility on Christmas Island, 1400km off Australia's northwest coast. Construction began in January 2005, with the facility scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson stated the facility would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre, and that a review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents were concerned about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and lack of consultation. He said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals sought written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett said transferring asylum seekers to the remote location denied them proper processing and legal access. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's decision to exempt itself from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

reconstructed_article: Democrats.com, a progressive organization, is offering a $1,000 reward to anyone who can get U.S. President George W. Bush to answer a question about pre-war intelligence. The offer follows a month during which Bush did not answer questions about a leaked secret memo stating that “the intelligence and facts were being fixed around the policy.” Neither the U.S. nor UK government has disputed the document’s accuracy. The question asks whether Bush and his administration “fixed” intelligence about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and terrorism ties to justify the invasion of Iraq. An additional $100 is offered to anyone who asks Bush the question, with video evidence required. The reward money came from modest donations to the website. The contest occurs amid renewed criticism from citizens, members of Congress, retired politicians, and constitutional lawyers following the leak of British documents. The report states that although efforts have been taken to combat corruption, ridding it completely will be difficult. It notes that since relevant mechanisms and systems are still incomplete, corruption persists, with some cases involving huge sums of money. The situation in combating corruption remains very serious, and the tasks are still substantial.

reconstructed_article: Sam Savarino, developer and CEO of Savarino Companies, confirmed he purchased a severely damaged stable and livery on Buffalo’s West Side from owner Bob Freudenheim for $1.00 and plans to restore it. The building partially collapsed on June 11, causing 15 homes to be evacuated. Savarino stated he hopes to save the facade, at least 20 feet of the side walls, all of the back walls including the elevator tower, and, if possible, all three floors. He inherits a tax lien of over $400,000 against the property, which represents the cost the city was billed for limited demolition work performed before the purchase. The city is suing Freudenheim to recover those fees. The building is undergoing minor demolition to shore up the remaining structure. Savarino’s tentative plans include living units on two floors with parking on the ground floor. Construction could begin as early as this year, but more likely next year. The project is estimated to cost at least $3,500,000. All plans must be approved by the city’s planning board. The city had originally ordered an emergency demolition after Freudenheim gave permission on June 12 during an emergency Preservation Board meeting, stating he would not rehabilitate the building. Residents obtained a restraining order to halt demolition. The next hearing is scheduled for September 2.

Savarino stated he hopes to save the facade, at least 20 feet of the side walls, all of the back walls including the elevator tower, and if possible all three floors. He inherits a burdensome tax lien of over $400,000 against the property, which represents the cost the city was billed for limited demolition work performed before the purchase. The city is currently suing Freudenheim to recover those fees. The building is undergoing minor demolition to shore up the remaining structure. Savarino's uncertain tentative plans include living units on two floors with parking on the ground floor. Construction could begin as early as this year, but more likely next year. The project is estimated to cost at least a daunting $3,500,000, and all plans must be approved by the city's planning board. The city had originally ordered an emergency demolition after Freudenheim gave permission on June 12 during an emergency Preservation Board meeting, stating he would not rehabilitate the building. Residents obtained a restraining order to halt demolition. The next hearing is scheduled for September 2.

reconstructed_article: On Thursday, the Taiwan External Trade Development Council (TAITRA) announced the winners of the Gold and Silver Awards at the 2008 16th-annual Taiwan Excellence Awards, held at the Taipei International Convention Center. TAITRA organized the event, which was created to promote products made in Taiwan. This year, 601 products competed for eight gold medals and twenty-one silver awards. In the ICT category, 388 products were on display from the industry. In total, 308 products from 102 companies were entitled as “Taiwan Excellent Products.” Several world-class experts judged the nominated products, selecting the final twenty-nine based on four critical factors. TAITRA also had categories where people could vote over the Internet or using their mobile phones. ASUSTeK Computer Incorporated received two Gold Awards and six Silver Awards. The ASUS Eee PC 4G, with features including mobility, reliability, and connectivity, won a Gold Award and was voted “Most Popular Product” by Internet and mobile users. ASUSTeK Computer Incorporated received the Taiwan Excellence Best Performance Award, while D-Link Corporation received the Taiwan Excellence Achievement Award. Gold Award winners included the ASUS R700t portable navigation device, AverVision SPB350, N133I6 ultra-slim wide LCD panel, MBA-00 Glee Cube multimedia IP-TV box, P3650 Touch Cruise, Hiwin E2 ecological and economical lubrication module, and Merida Ninety Six carbon full suspension. Silver Award winners included products from ASUS, Gigabyte, Panasonic, D-Link, ZyXEL, Giant, and others across multiple categories.

reconstructed_article: Australian transport investigators identified a safety issue with engines fitted to Airbus A380 passenger airliners. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said some Rolls-Royce Trent 900 engines may be prone to fatigue cracking, which could lead to oil leakage and fire. The ATSB said this was central to the engine failure on a Qantas A380 on November 4, shortly after take-off from Singapore. Qantas grounded all six of its A380 fleet for safety checks before returning them to service. The ATSB said the fault could lead to an elevated risk of fatigue crack initiation and growth, oil leakage, and a resulting oil fire. The agency, which is responsible for such investigations, urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Qantas stated there was no immediate risk to flight safety but would conduct further investigations. Two A380 aircraft were in operational service, with both to be inspected at the Qantas Jet Base in Sydney. Two other airlines, Lufthansa and Singapore Airlines, use A380 aircraft with Trent engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' can carry 450.

reconstructed_article: At the end of January, Bach Technology announced MusicDNA, a new music file format intended as a replacement for the MP3 format. MusicDNA uses compression methods similar to MP3 but adds an XML file that defines additional content, including lyrics, artwork, tour dates, blog posts, videos, and Twitter feeds. The files also contain audio analysis information intended to improve search, recommendation, and playlist tools. Bach Technology CEO Stefan Kohlmeyer stated that MusicDNA has been in development since the company's founding in 2007. Bach holds a strategic partnership with Fraunhofer IDMT, whose CEO Karlheinz Brandenburg, credited with inventing the MP3, participates in research and development discussions. Unlike iTunes LP, MusicDNA is built on open standards and is platform-agnostic, allowing transfer between devices and purchase of individual tracks rather than complete albums. Additional content updates dynamically when the user is online. Only paid files receive dynamic updates, which Bach Technology describes as an incentive to purchase legitimate files rather than using peer-to-peer networks. Mark Mulligan, vice president and research director at Forrester Research, told a UK newspaper that innovations like iTunes LP need to go further, suggesting people should pay once for regularly updated content. Kohlmeyer noted that MP3 was developed over twenty years ago and does little to add to the listening experience beyond portability. MusicDNA rollout is staggered over 2010, with beta versions around Easter and full commercial rollout expected in summer.

Alan Winters, professor of economics at the University of Sussex and founding director of the UK Trade Policy Observatory (UKTPO), was interviewed about UK trade policy following Brexit. Winters stated he was opposed to Brexit and considers it poor economic policy, arguing the UK would have been better off with a tighter relationship with Europe to keep trade costs lower. He co-authored reports including "The Costs of Brexit," "COVID-19 will reinforce the Brexit shock," and "Taking stock of the new UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement." Winters said Brexit and COVID-19 shocks interact, making recovery from lost export markets harder. He dismissed the idea that trade with distant partners like Australia, New Zealand, or CPTPP members could replace EU trade, noting the EU represents approximately half of UK trade and that benefits of trade agreements weaken with distance. On fishing, he noted the UK gained some quota transfer but must still prove compliance with EU standards to sell fish in Europe. He criticized government statistics presenting £218 billion in rolled-over trade as new income. Regarding the Northern Ireland Protocol, he attributed complications to Brexit and the specific form of Brexit chosen by Boris Johnson. Winters argued the UK should pursue a quiet, cooperative role in the WTO and urged the G7 to focus on repairing the multilateral trading system rather than pursuing bilateral photo opportunities. He expressed concern about rising Chinese-Western tensions and cautioned against framing democratic cooperation in an anti-China light. He called for greater domestic debate on trade policy, noting the executive faces few constraints.

reconstructed_article: Roger D. Kornberg of the United States won the 2006 Nobel Prize for chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. Kornberg’s work explains how information encoded in DNA is used to produce the proteins that keep cells functioning. Eukaryotes are multi-celled organisms, such as animals, plants and fungi, which have their genetic material stored in nuclei within their cells. To use their genetic information, eukaryotes extract bits of the coded information via the formation of messenger RNA, which consists of copies of a particular gene within the DNA strand. Translation takes place when proteins are built from the information transcribed with the messenger RNA. Eukaryotic transcription is vital for life. If transcription is interrupted, as can happen when cells are exposed to certain toxins, the cells will die. Kornberg documented eukaryotic transcription with snapshots of the process in action. He created the snapshots by crystallizing cellular material partway through transcription and exposing them to x-rays that produced patterns revealing the intermediate structures. Kornberg’s work may lead to novel drugs and medical treatments. Kornberg’s father Arthur Kornberg won the Nobel Prize in physiology and medicine in 1959 for explaining how organisms synthesize DNA from nucleotides.

reconstructed_article: American botanist Lou Jost has discovered the world's smallest orchid among the roots of a larger plant in a nature reserve in Ecuador. The flowers measure 2.1mm wide and have transparent petals that are one cell thick. The finding surpasses the previous record held by Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo, Japan, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages from the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers. The class action is the first in Japan related to health damages caused by asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas. The plaintiffs claim the government and manufacturers knew of the dangers of asbestos inhalation but failed to take proper precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died. The plaintiffs argue the government and health ministry did not act quickly enough after international organizations issued warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen. They also blame the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for approving asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law. Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. Following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, the government implemented a 2006 law providing monetary assistance to victims and relatives. The plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

The commitment was made in Thailand at Asia's first ministerial conference on tiger conservation. The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found. Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva stated in a video address that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it. The meeting was partially organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups. Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared to about 3,500 today. According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago, according to Voice of America. WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

The contest follows Bush’s month-long period without answering questions about a leaked secret memo stating that “the intelligence and facts were being fixed around the policy.” Neither the U.S. nor UK government has disputed the document’s accuracy. The question asks whether Bush and his administration “fixed” intelligence about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and terrorism ties to justify the invasion of Iraq. An additional $100 is offered to anyone who asks Bush the question, with video evidence required. The reward money came from small donations to the website. The contest occurs amid renewed criticism from citizens, members of Congress, retired politicians, and constitutional lawyers following the leak of British documents. Earlier in the month, White House spokesman Scott McClellan told reporters the administration saw “no need” to respond to a congressional letter about the memo, stating that public comments before the war showed how intelligence was used. One pre-war justification was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, none of which were found. The Senate Intelligence Committee is considering three possibilities: the weapons were moved, CIA intelligence was flawed, or satisfactory intelligence was mishandled by the administration. The last possibility has not been formally investigated.

reconstructed_article: Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that it may be forced to mothball its steelworks in Teesside, England, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. Corus may close its Teesside operations because a consortium has refused to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations. Corus’ chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

reconstructed_article: NASA disclosed that a three-inch gouge was found in the heat shield on one of Endeavour's wings. The gouge was observed as the shuttle approached the International Space Station (ISS) and was captured on camera by ISS astronauts. According to NASA, the gouge was located on a six-inch thick tile on the starboard wing of the heat shield and may have been caused by ice rather than foam. NASA expressed concern because the hole appears to be deep. Mission management team chairman John Shannon stated that the assessment would involve thermal analysis based on the damage, a review of flight history, and testing of the area. He noted that it was too early to determine whether repairs were required. If the damage is irreversible and cannot be fixed, the Endeavour crew would remain on the ISS. NASA stated that supplies would last until a rescue mission could be launched on October 8. During Endeavour's liftoff on August 8, cameras showed moisture on the lens, but the object causing the damage was not captured. At least nine pieces of debris were filmed during takeoff, though NASA said only three had a possibility of hitting the shuttle. Astronauts were expected to use a laser attached to the shuttle's robotic arm to measure the gouge's depth and size on Sunday. Potential repairs included affixing a metal plate over the tile, filling it with putty, or sealing the gouge.

reconstructed_article: The World Bank released its 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report mentions India 300 times, Spain 48 times, Canada 22 times, and New Zealand 15 times. The report states that gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making. In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman's income correlated positively with years her children spent in school. No gender gap exists in school attendance for the richest 20% of Indian families, but among the poorest 20%, males outnumber females 5 to 1 in attendance. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1; males average completion of Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones. Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. A fifth of married Indian women do not control household spending decisions, an average of 18% matching Mozambique, between Nigeria at 14% and Zambia and Rwanda at 20%. India reduced average children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India's maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China they grew by 202,000.

reconstructed_article: A paper published earlier this week by the US-based Center for Global Development estimated that excess deaths in India during the COVID-19 pandemic numbered between 3.4 million and 5 million between May 2020 and June 21, 2021. The estimate was calculated using death certificates from seven states, international estimates of age-specific infection rates compared to antibody test data, and a consumer survey recording deaths. The researchers noted that while not all excess deaths were necessarily caused by COVID-19, the metric can help calculate the pandemic's impact. The researchers stated the death toll was likely to be far greater than the official count and likely to be in the millions. A co-writer of the report said that after the first wave—which was more spread out—undercounting of deaths led to a culture of complacency, but the second wave galvanised Indian society to investigate the numbers. The co-writer added that the figures only went up to May and did not include all of June or any of July, meaning the true death toll may still be undercounted. More than 414,000 COVID-19 deaths have been officially recorded in India, the third-highest total in the world. There is no official record of excess deaths in India during the pandemic.

reconstructed_article: International twin-study researchers conducted parallel genetic studies into bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, examining more than 50,000 people worldwide. Eleven genetic regions were identified; seven were for schizophrenia, five of which were previously undiscovered. Two genetic loci were associated with both diseases. The studies scanned genomes of both healthy and afflicted individuals. Researchers found that genetic factors are numerous rather than a single faulty gene. In schizophrenia, at most around 30% of genetic components are thought to have been identified. Pablo Gejman, a lead researcher on the schizophrenia study, stated that one goal of genetic research is to find druggable targets. He identified calcium-activated channels in the brain as promising candidates for new drugs, linked to schizophrenia in the study. A genetic locus called mir137 suggests an abnormality of gene regulation. The team found no evidence that dopamine receptors are involved, though current drug treatments target them. Professor Rodney Scott from the University of Newcastle in Australia noted the strength of the research lies in its numbers, providing robust statistical power. Both Gejman and Scott described the study as highly reliable due to its sample size. Scott noted that the two shared genetic loci are suggestive of a potential common pathway giving rise to both diseases. Gejman called it an excellent demonstration because the same chains are common to both disorders. Each illness affects approximately 1% of people. The diseases are poorly understood, and it remains uncertain whether they are components of a single spectrum or comprise multiple illnesses.

reconstructed_article: The University of Southern California developed a simulation system called Virtual Iraq, designed to provide battlefield effects. reconstructed_article: On Tuesday, the World Bank released the 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report uses the United States as a benchmark for understanding gains for women globally and notes that US women still lag behind US men in several areas. The report finds that US women are disproportionately represented in teaching and nursing, are paid less than male counterparts, and are under-represented at the highest business levels, with only 28 of Fortune 1000 companies having a female CEO. Women in the bottom 20% economically have a slightly higher birth rate than those in the top 20%. Immigrants from Southeast Asia and India show higher than expected male-to-female birth ratios, which the report attributes partly to deliberate sex selection based on cultural attitudes. In 2009, over half a million US women were victims of intimate partner violence. US men hold greater pension assets, and elderly women are more likely to live alone than with a spouse. Women account for less than 20% of local police officers and bear 61% of housework duties. High childcare costs discourage women from re-entering the workforce after giving birth. The report notes that major gains took considerable time: it took 40 years (1870–1910) to see meaningful improvements in girls’ school attendance aged 6–12. In 1921, after women obtained suffrage, Congress passed legislation that helped lower infant mortality from 23% to 15%. Property rights for women began by 1848 in New York. The report cites research showing that higher maternal education improves children’s outcomes.

Icelandic boys' and girls' mathematics test scores were nearly identical, around 510, with boys slightly higher. Girls outperformed boys on literacy, approximately 525 to 480. Girls' mathematics performance was similar to Estonia, Germany, and Belgium; literacy performance was similar to Sweden, Poland, Switzerland, Estonia, and Belgium. Iceland's mortality rate per 1,000 people aged 15–60 was 56, compared to the United States at 107, China at 113, India at 213, Iraq at 285, Afghanistan at 479, Malawi at 481, and Zimbabwe at 772. The report notes that Iceland not being in a conflict or HIV/AIDS-affected country is a contributing reason. Iceland was one of 23 countries with over 30% female parliamentary representation, alongside Rwanda, Argentina, Cuba, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden. In the mid-1990s, only 5 countries met this threshold. The report highlights the 1983 creation of an all-women's political party as increasing attention to women's issues. Icelandic women in both private and public sectors earn approximately 22% less than men.

reconstructed_article: U.S. federal agents arrested Dang Vang, 48, at his Fresno home. A federal grand jury indicted 11 men, including former Royal Lao Army general and Hmong leader Vang Pao, 77, on charges connected to a plot by 10 of them to overthrow the government of Laos. The men are charged with violating the U.S. Neutrality Act, which prohibits using United States soil to conspire to overthrow a foreign government with peaceful relations with the U.S. U.S. Attorney McGregor Scott stated that federal law prohibits conspiring to overthrow a foreign government with whom the nation is at peace. According to the ATF, Dang Vang wrote the group’s action plan, which summarized a plot to blow up government buildings in Laos and assassinate government officials. The plot was named Operation Popcorn, or Political Opposition Party’s Coup Operation to Rescue a Nation. Those charged also include Harrison Jack, 60, a retired California National Guard colonel and Vietnam War veteran; Lo Cha Thao, 34; Lo Thao, 53, of Sacramento; Youa True Vang, 60, of Fresno; Hue Vang, 39, of Fresno; Chong Vang Thao, 53, of Fresno; Seng Vue, 68, of Fresno; Chue Lo, 59; and Nhia Kao Vang, 48. Most of those indicted are prominent members of the Hmong immigrant community in California’s Central Valley.

reconstructed_article: An 11-year-old girl, Maribel Cuevas, faces felony assault charges in California after throwing a stone at a group of boys who were throwing water balloons at her. In April, Cuevas was taken into custody by Fresno, California police and spent five days in juvenile hall after throwing the stone at the group of boys who bombarded her with water balloons as she walked down the sidewalk. A 9-year-old boy was hit with the stone and suffered a wound to his head requiring medical assistance. Since then, Cuevas has spent one month under house arrest pending court. Cuevas’ lawyer, Richard Beshwate, told the BBC that “They [Fresno police] are treating her like a violent parole offender. It’s not a felony, it’s an 11-year-old acting like an 11-year-old.” Fresno Police Sergeant Anthony Martinez told reporters: “We responded. We determined a felony assault had taken place and the officers took the actions that were necessary.” Cuevas is due back in court next month on felony assault charges. During her five-day detention, she was placed in juvenile hall and allowed one 30-minute visit from her parents. She was then placed under 30-day house arrest and required to wear an electronic monitoring bracelet. The house arrest allowed her to attend school. Maribel, who knows very little English, said that the boy initiated the conflict—the boy also admitted as much.

Gardaí fired several shots at the driver’s tires and laid tacks on the road. The bus travelled down the wrong side of the N7, where it collided with a number of cars, killing a female driver, and rammed five Garda patrol cars that were blocking the road. The driver was apprehended and arrested at the Dualway depot after the bus crashed. One person is dead and 13 others, including 5 members of the Garda Síochána, are injured. Sections of the N7 as well as surrounding roads were closed following the incident for forensic examinations, and tram services were severely curtailed.

reconstructed_article: U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon’s song “Imagine” in the film “Expelled” is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film, produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as “the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion.” In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical “Imagine there’s no heaven … and no religion too.” On April 23, 2008, Lennon’s widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense Premise Media had advanced would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that “the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright.” “Expelled” is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. It has received criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced copyright claims over animated sequences resembling “The Inner Life of the Cell,” produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that “it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners” and plans to appeal.

In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." It has received criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

reconstructed_article: Matthew Wright, host of British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks made on the show regarding the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the edition broadcast on Tuesday, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. mobilized in response to the sighting, coordinating an effort to protect the animals. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, were deployed by authorities and used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., authorities and volunteers had guided the whales back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in the film "Expelled" is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking substantial damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." "Expelled" is a documentary that claims intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. Scientists and film critics have criticized the film. The film has faced additional copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

reconstructed_article: Dr. Stephen Schoenthaler, Professor of Criminal Justice at California State University in Stanislaus, has advanced the argument that there is a link between a healthy diet and decreased aggressive behaviour, as well as increased IQ and school performance. In a study he conducted in a youth detention center, violations of house rules fell by 37% when vending machines were removed and the cafeteria replaced canned food with fresh alternatives. Schoenthaler states that having a bad diet is a better predictor of future violence than past violent behaviour. He also directed a study across 803 New York City schools in low-income neighbourhoods, finding that the number of students passing final exams increased by 16%. Critics have questioned some of Schoenthaler's findings due to the lack of placebo control groups. More recent work by Dr. Bernard Gesch, a physiologist at the University of Oxford, found that nutrition supplements produced a 26% drop in violations of prison rules over a placebo and a 37% decrease in violent offences. The Netherlands has embarked on a wider-scale dietary research program in 14 prisons. reconstructed_article: Corus, the world’s fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that its steelworks in Teesside, England, may be mothballed, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. The closure of Corus’ Teesside operations may be forced by a consortium’s refusal to honour a 10-year contract with Corus’ Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant’s operations. Corus’ chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government’s assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. reconstructed_article: After Atlanta, Georgia lost its bid to host Wikimania 2008, which was awarded to Alexandria, Egypt, organizers began planning a Conference of the Americas focused on Wikimedia in the Americas. The conference is scheduled for May 15–18, 2008, at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta. One organizer, an unpaid intern at the Wikimedia Foundation offices in St. Petersburg, Florida, stated that planning discussions began before the Wikimania location was announced and that the conference was not created in retaliation or to compete with Wikimania. He said the goal is to provide a Wikimedia event for the western hemisphere, noting that travel to Egypt is more expensive for people in the region. Over 100 interested parties across the United States have expressed interest in volunteering or attending. Wikimedia and the free culture movement will be covered by the conference in relation to communities in North America, including the United States and Canada, and Latin America. A journalism segment will be held at the Turner Broadcasting building on Techwood Drive in Midtown Atlanta. The Wikimedia Foundation and Wikimedia Argentina have received proposals for endorsement, with decisions pending. Georgia Tech, the Public Journalism Network, and the Carolina Open Source Initiative sponsor the conference. The selection of Alexandria for Wikimania 2008 prompted discussion on public mailing lists regarding safety, free speech, and the jury's decision process.

reconstructed_article: Police in Purcell, Oklahoma, approximately 40 miles (64 km) south of Oklahoma City, discovered the body of ten-year-old Jamie Rose Bolin on Friday in the apartment of Kevin Underwood, 26, a resident of the same apartment complex. Tim Kuykendall, district attorney for McClain County, said the body was found in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Underwood was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail, pending further proceedings. He had no known prior criminal record or history of mental illness. Bolin was last seen on Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting that no abduction had been reported initially. Underwood only came under suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex. Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment. Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body suggested an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected possible postmortem molestation, as the body was found unclothed. Purcell police chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Kuykendall said Underwood reported fantasizing about eating someone beginning a year prior. Authorities believed other individuals, including a woman and a 5-year-old boy, may have been targeted and considered. Kuykendall stated he intended to seek the death penalty.
